title: 3-Read Friday #100: Instructional Design Failure, Reduced Feedback, and Ditching QLA
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue #100 of 3-Read Friday leads with Kris Boulton's argument that when students repeatedly fail at multi-step processes, the fault usually lies in instructional design rather than student ability -- and that identifying which tasks are genuinely multi-step 'cognitive routines' is the essential first step to teaching them well. Paul Kirschner then makes the case for reduced feedback as an underrated desirable difficulty: deliberately fading the frequency and specificity of feedback forces students to build the internal monitoring and self-correction skills that durable, transferable learning depends on, provided they already have enough foundational knowledge to benefit from the struggle. Joel Kenyon closes by dismantling Question Level Analysis (QLA) spreadsheets, arguing they create an illusion of analytic precision while wasting teacher time and conflating performance with learning, and should be replaced by ongoing formative assessment and targeted spaced retrieval. Barton frames all three as attacks on comfortable but flawed proxies -- for ability, for support, and for data -- in favour of harder, more accurate alternatives.
points: Boulton reframes 'some children will always fail' as a design problem: failure at multi-step tasks is usually a symptom of unidentified cognitive routines within the task, not a fixed trait of the student.

Kirschner's reduced-feedback argument has a crucial precondition -- fading feedback only builds self-monitoring skill when students already hold enough foundational knowledge to make productive use of the resulting struggle.
Kenyon's critique of QLA spreadsheets is that they manufacture false precision and eat teacher time better spent on formative assessment and spaced retrieval -- precision theatre, not precision.

The shared thread across all three posts: comfortable proxies (student ability, constant feedback, spreadsheet data) routinely substitute for the harder, more accurate diagnostic work good teaching actually requires.
quotes: A powerful post from Kris that encapsulates his whole unstoppable learning philosophy.
